title: Sealed replay and scoring

story: BYTE-GOLD, the answer key for Byte, our review agent, is ready: 240 old PRs from fcp, our product repo, each with the bugs a good reviewer should find. You replay Byte on all of them, and the first number is wonderful: Byte caught 94% of the high bugs. Then you open the log of one case. Byte was reviewing PR #1874 from last spring, and the checkout still had fcp's full history. One of its first commands was git log on the file it was reading, and the newest commit there was the fix: Dataset check uses the dataset's workgroup. Byte did not find the bug. It read the answer.

This is not a strange accident. When researchers sealed the environment of a well-known coding benchmark, so that agents could no longer fetch the real fix from git history or the web, scores dropped noticeably. A test that lets the student see the future measures nothing.
hook.question: How do we let Byte review an old PR exactly as it was then, with no way to see what happened after?

read.h: Three ways the future leaks in
p: When Byte reviews an old PR in a normal setup, the future can reach it in three ways. The first is the git history: a clone of fcp contains every later commit, including the fix and its message. The second is the GitHub token: with a live token, Byte can read the PR's later comments, the linked fix PR, even a revert. A live token is also dangerous the other way round, because a replay would post new review comments on a PR that was merged a year ago. The third is the network: from the internet, the fix is one search away.

So a replay is sealed: we close all three doors, and we do it without changing Byte. The score should describe the Byte we really ship, so the replay runs the same worker image, the same model and the same flags as a live review. Only what Byte can reach is different. It is like an exam room: the student is the same person, but the phone and the notes stay outside. Unlike an exam room, one door stays open, to the Claude API, because Byte cannot think without it.

read.h: The pack: the PR as it was
p: A pack is a folder holding everything Byte needs to review one old PR, and nothing else. It has three files. diff.patch is what the PR changed. tree.tar holds the files at the PR's head commit, made with git archive, which writes the files but not the .git folder, so there is no history to read. pr.json holds the PR's title and body, its file list with line counts, its SHAs, and the flags Byte's gate would pass for fcp.

For a planted case, the packer applies planted.patch on the head before it writes the tree, and adds it to the diff, so Byte sees the bug as if the author had written it. If the PR's body was edited later and mentions the bug (blankBody in the case file), the body is left out.

code.file: what the packer does for one case (byte gold-pack)
code.text:
# one case: the introducing PR's base and head, from a shallow fetch of fcp
git diff "$base...$head" > pack/input/diff.patch     # what the PR changed
git archive "$head" -o pack/input/tree.tar           # the files at head, and no .git folder
gh api "repos/RhinoHealth/fcp/pulls/$pr" > pr.raw.json
# pr.json keeps: title, body (left out when blankBody is true), files with
# additions and deletions, base and head SHAs, and reviewArgs: the flags the
# gate would pass for fcp, so the replay runs the way production runs

notes.text: git archive exports the files of one commit. The .git folder, and with it every later commit, never enters the pack.
The PR's metadata comes from GitHub when the pack is built, by a token that never enters a container.

read.h: A broker that answers from the pack
p: Byte's worker never calls GitHub itself; it asks the broker, which holds the token. That design is what makes sealing easy. For a replay we start the same broker class with an empty token and two injected functions. Reads are answered from the pack: the diff, the PR view, the file list. The lists of earlier reviews and comments are always empty, because every replay is a first review, and anything the pack cannot answer is refused. Writes are recorded in publication.json instead of being posted.
The worker cannot tell the difference. It sends the same gh commands as in a live review and gets answers in the same shape, so the review runs exactly as it would on a new PR.

notes.text: No token at all. Even a bug in this file cannot leak one or reach GitHub.
Earlier reviews and comments: always none. Real ones could quote the bug or the fix.
Anything else is refused, so a new kind of read shows up as a failure instead of a silent leak.
Byte's review lands in a file for scoring. Nothing is ever posted on the old PR.

p: The last door is the network. The replay script creates a Docker network with the internal flag, which means containers on it can talk to each other but have no route to anything outside. The broker and the worker live only there. The one exception is a Squid proxy, the same kind of allow-list proxy our VMs use: it is connected to the internal network and to Docker's normal bridge network, and its allow-list has a single host, api.anthropic.com. The worker reaches Claude through it, and nothing else.

The answer key is never mounted into any container, and every container runs with the same hardening flags as a live review: no Linux capabilities, a read-only file system, no privilege escalation. A trap at the end of the script removes the containers and the network, whatever happens.

code.text:
docker network create --internal "$net"     # nothing on it has a route out

# squid: on the internal network AND the default bridge, allows api.anthropic.com only
docker run -d --name "ge-$id" --network "$net" --read-only --tmpfs /var/spool/squid --tmpfs /var/run \
  -v "$PWD/config/gold-squid.conf:/etc/squid/squid.conf:ro" "$SQUID_IMAGE"
docker network connect bridge "ge-$id"

# the replay broker: the pack, read-only, and no token
docker run -d --name "gb-$id" --network "$net" --cap-drop ALL --read-only --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -e BYTE_BROKER_CAPABILITY="$cap" -v "$pack/input:/input:ro" -v "$out/$id:/output" \
  "$image" broker --replay /input

# the real worker image, reviewing the tree with no .git
docker run --rm --network "$net" --cap-drop ALL --read-only --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -e HTTPS_PROXY="http://ge-$id:3128" -e BYTE_BROKER_URL="http://gb-$id:8080" -e BYTE_BROKER_CAPABILITY="$cap" \
  -v "$tree:/workspace:ro" -v "$out/$id:/output" -w /workspace \
  "$image" review "${review_args[@]}" --check-id 0 --output-directory /output

notes.text: --internal: no route out. A container here cannot reach the internet or your laptop's other networks.
The only container on both networks, so the only way out, and it allows one host.
The pack is mounted read-only. The byte-gold repo, with the answers, is mounted nowhere.
The tree from tree.tar, read-only, with no .git folder.

read.h: From replays to a score, and a gate
p: Each sealed replay leaves a publication.json with Byte's findings. Scoring compares them with the golden comments in two steps. Code first keeps only pairs that could match: same file, and a finding line within 10 lines of the golden range. Then a small, cheap model call, a judge, answers one yes-or-no question per pair: does this finding describe this defect? From the matches come the numbers: recall (the share of known bugs Byte caught) for high, medium and low bugs, precision (how many of Byte's findings matched a real or planted bug), and false alarms per clean PR.

Those numbers become a gate: a required check in Byte's repo that replays the cases whenever a PR changes Byte's prompts, playbooks, model or effort. The change fails if recall on high bugs drops more than 3 points below the last main run, or if clean PRs get more than 0.2 false alarms each. From now on, a rule or a cheaper setting stays in Byte only if BYTE-GOLD says it still catches the bugs.

deeper.h: Go deeper: trusting the judge, and keeping the test fair
p: The judge is Haiku 5.5 at low effort with no tools. Before the gate trusts it, two people label 50 finding-and-golden pairs by hand; if the judge agrees with them less than 90% of the time, it moves to Sonnet 5.5 at medium. The scorecard holds numbers only, never a path or code, like Byte's other telemetry.

The cases are split once, by a stable hash of the case id, into a dev split (two thirds) that every PR replays and a holdout split (one third) that runs once a month. Nobody tunes Byte against the holdout, so it shows whether Byte was tuned, by accident, to fit the dev cases only. A PR that only changes one team's playbook replays only that team's cases, to keep cost down. Before anything runs, a leak check fails the job if a case's PR number, head SHA or Jira key appears in Byte's playbooks, because the weekly loop writes lessons from live reviews into them. Main is replayed three times first to measure noise, because two runs of the same model never give exactly the same answers.

lab.title: Close the three doors
needs: The gold-lab repo from the g2-1 lab
lab.goal: See the future leak in a normal clone, then build a pack with no history and a Docker network whose only way out is a one-host proxy.

guess.q: You unpack tree.tar into a folder and run git log there. What happens?

options.text: It shows the PR's own commits only
options.why: git archive copies files, not commits. There is no history of any kind in the tree.

options.text: It fails with not a git repository, as long as the folder is not inside another git repo
options.why: No .git folder, no history. But git also searches parent folders, which is why the tree must live outside any clone; the Fix step shows that trap.

options.text: It shows the full fcp history
options.why: That would be true for a clone. An archive is only the files of one commit.

follow.say: First see the leak. Check out PR #12's head in the full clone, the way a careless replay would, and ask git about the file.
follow.do:
cd ~/academy-labs/scratch/gold-lab && git switch -q --detach ":/RH-1207" && git log --oneline -1
git log --oneline --all -- src/paging.ts | head -1
git switch -q main
follow.see:
fcb91e8 [FE] RH-1207: Projects table pages through every project (#12)
fc403bc [FE] RH-1301: Every page shows 25 projects, not 26 (#15)

follow.say: Build a pack for PR #12 outside the clone: the diff against its base, and the files at its head with no .git.
follow.do:
base=$(git log --format=%H --grep='(#11)'); head=$(git log --format=%H --grep='(#12)')
pack=~/academy-labs/scratch/pack-real-0001 && mkdir -p $pack/input $pack/tree
git diff "$base...$head" > $pack/input/diff.patch
git archive "$head" -o $pack/input/tree.tar && tar -xf $pack/input/tree.tar -C $pack/tree
ls -a $pack/tree && git -C $pack/tree log --oneline
follow.see:
.
..
src
fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git

follow.say: Mount the tree read-only into a container with no network at all, the way the worker sees /workspace, and try again.
follow.see:
fatal: not a git repository (or any parent up to mount point /)
Stopping at filesystem boundary (GIT_DISCOVERY_ACROSS_FILESYSTEM not set).

follow.say: Now the network. Create an internal network and try to reach the internet from it.
follow.do:
docker network create --internal gold-sealed
docker run --rm --network gold-sealed curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -sS --max-time 5 https://example.com -o /dev/null; echo "exit $?"
follow.see:
curl: (28) Resolving timed out after 5003 milliseconds
exit 28

follow.say: Open one door: a Squid proxy on both networks that allows a single host. In Byte that host is api.anthropic.com; here it is example.com.
follow.do:
cd ~/academy-labs/scratch && mkdir -p seal && cd seal && cat > squid.conf <<'EOF'
http_port 3128
dns_nameservers 1.1.1.1
acl allowed dstdomain example.com
http_access allow CONNECT allowed
http_access deny all
EOF
docker run -d --name gold-proxy --network gold-sealed -v "$PWD/squid.conf:/etc/squid/squid.conf:ro" ubuntu/squid:latest
docker network connect bridge gold-proxy

follow.say: Try the allowed host and a forbidden one through the proxy, then read Squid's log, which is the evidence a smoke test checks.
follow.do:
for u in https://example.com https://github.com; do docker run --rm --network gold-sealed curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -sS --max-time 10 -x http://gold-proxy:3128 -o /dev/null -w "$u %{http_code}\n" $u; done
docker exec gold-proxy tail -2 /var/log/squid/access.log
follow.see:
https://example.com 200
curl: (56) CONNECT tunnel failed, response 403
https://github.com 000
... TCP_TUNNEL/200 5415 CONNECT example.com:443 - HIER_DIRECT/172.66.147.243 -
... TCP_DENIED/403 3392 CONNECT github.com:443 - HIER_NONE/- text/html

lab.build: Pack the planted case from the g2-1 lab, cases/planted-0001, whose head is PR #11. The tree must hold the files at #11's head with planted.patch applied, and diff.patch must hold #11's change followed by the planted patch (#11 is the first commit, so use git show --format= on it instead of a base...head diff). Check that the tree's src/paging.ts contains rows.slice(1, PAGE_SIZE) and that diff.patch has two diff --git lines. Then clean up: docker rm -f gold-proxy and docker network rm gold-sealed.
checks: In the full clone, git log --all shows the fix commit (#15) while you are on PR #12's head.
git log in the unpacked tree fails with not a git repository.
curl from the internal network without the proxy times out.
Through the proxy, example.com answers 200 and github.com is refused with 403, and Squid's log shows both.
Your planted pack's tree contains the planted bug, and its diff.patch has two diff --git lines.

solution.text:
head=$(git log --format=%H --grep='(#11)')
p=~/academy-labs/scratch/pack-planted-0001 && mkdir -p $p/input $p/tree
git archive "$head" | tar -x -C $p/tree
(cd $p/tree && git apply ~/academy-labs/scratch/gold-lab/cases/planted-0001/planted.patch)
{ git show --format= "$head"; cat cases/planted-0001/planted.patch; } > $p/input/diff.patch
tar -cf $p/input/tree.tar -C $p/tree .
grep slice $p/tree/src/paging.ts        # rows.slice(1, PAGE_SIZE)
grep -c '^diff --git' $p/input/diff.patch   # 2
docker rm -f gold-proxy && docker network rm gold-sealed

lab.fix: A teammate's packer unpacks the tree into gold-lab/pack/tree, inside the clone, "to keep things together". Try it: mkdir -p pack/tree && tar -xf ~/academy-labs/scratch/pack-real-0001/input/tree.tar -C pack/tree && git -C pack/tree log --oneline | head -1. The fix commit appears again. Explain why (git looks for a .git folder in every parent folder) and repair it, then delete pack/.
explain: Name the three ways the future can reach Byte during a replay, and what closes each one.
Why does the replay run Byte's real worker image instead of a simpler test version?
Why does the replay broker answer the lists of earlier reviews and comments with an empty list?
lab.done: Your pack has no history, the internal network has one way out to one host, you packed the planted case, and you removed the proxy and the network.

check.q: Why is the tree in a pack made with git archive instead of a clone checked out at the PR's head?

options.text: git archive is faster for big repos
options.why: Speed is a side effect. The reason is what the archive leaves out.

options.text: A clone carries every later commit, including the fix, and git archive writes the files without any history
options.why: With no .git folder, git log has nothing to show, so the fix cannot be read.

options.text: The worker cannot read files from a clone
options.why: It can read any files. That is exactly the problem with a clone.

check.q: In a replay, Byte's worker asks the broker for the PR's earlier review comments. What does it get?

options.text: The comments that were really posted on the PR, read with a live token
options.why: There is no token, and real comments could describe the bug or link the fix.

options.text: An error that stops the replay
options.why: This read is expected in every review, so the replay broker answers it, just with nothing.

options.text: An empty list, because every replay is a first review
options.why: Byte reviews the PR as if it had just been opened, with nothing that came later.

check.q: Which container in a sealed replay can reach anything outside the internal network?

options.text: Only the Squid proxy, and it allows api.anthropic.com alone
options.why: It is the one container on both networks. The worker reaches Claude through it and nothing else.

options.text: The broker, because it must talk to GitHub
options.why: The replay broker answers from the pack. It has no token and no route out.

options.text: The worker, because the model runs there
options.why: The worker only reaches the broker and the proxy. Its calls to Claude go through Squid.

p: In RhinoHealth/byte: byte gold-pack (src/gold.ts) writes input/pr.json, diff.patch and tree.tar from a shallow fetch of the two SHAs; src/gold-broker.ts and byte broker --replay serve the pack with BYTE_BROKER_CAPABILITY and no BYTE_BROKER_TOKEN, which needs a new optional api injection in BrokerSessionOptions; scripts/gold-replay.sh reuses review.yml's container pattern with a per-run --internal network and a digest-pinned Squid allowing only api.anthropic.com (config/gold-squid.conf, from infrastructure's squid-proxy template without basic auth). Replays talk to Claude directly, as live Byte does; Byte does not use our gateway.

Scoring is byte gold-score (src/gold-score.ts) with a Haiku 5.5 judge, calibrated by Sean and Nave on 50 hand-labelled pairs. The gate is .github/workflows/gold.yml on byte-runner-set: it runs on PRs touching skills/**, src/engines.ts, src/limits.ts, src/review.ts, src/panel.ts, config/repositories.json or the Dockerfile, refreshes the baseline in data/gold-runs.jsonl on main, runs the holdout monthly, skips PRs opened by bots, and becomes a required check on byte's main.

tickets.why: The packer and the replay broker: no history, no token, publications recorded.
gold-replay.sh: the internal network, Squid with one host, the hardening flags, the smoke test on 5 packs.
Scoring: the line window, the judge and its calibration, the scorecard.
The gate in Byte's repo: splits, scope by change, the leak check and the pass bar.

words.plain: Running Byte on an old PR so that it can see the PR as it was, and nothing that happened later.
A folder with one PR's diff, its files at head (no .git) and its metadata: all Byte needs, nothing more.
Byte's normal broker with no token, answering reads from the pack and recording what Byte would post.
A Docker network whose containers can reach each other but have no route out.
A small model call that answers yes or no: does this finding describe this golden defect?
A required check that replays BYTE-GOLD and fails a change to Byte when quality drops.

review.q: From memory: the three files in a pack, and what each one leaves out on purpose.
review.a: diff.patch (the PR's change, plus planted.patch for a planted case), tree.tar (files at head, no .git, so no later history), pr.json (title, files, SHAs, review flags; the body is left out when blankBody is set).

review.q: A replay's Squid log shows a refused request to github.com. Is that a problem?
review.a: The seal worked, because the request was refused. But it means something in Byte tried to reach GitHub directly, which a smoke test should explain, since all GitHub reads should go to the replay broker.

review.q: Someone wants to make the replay faster by giving the worker a normal clone instead of tree.tar. What do you answer?
review.a: A clone contains the fix and every later commit, so Byte can read the answer with git log, and recall stops meaning anything.

remember: A replay measures Byte only if it is sealed: the files with no history, a broker with no token, and one door out to Claude.
